In [1], the emerging convergence between high-performance computing (HPC) and 
artificial intelligence (AI) was highlighted. At that time, the evolution of HPC hard-
ware, with GPUs and TPUs integrating as accelerators, fueled the rise of AI with 
dedicated deep learning models. This trend marked the beginning of a new approach 
to heterogeneous architectures, which became the fundamental basis for compute-
intensive applications.
Today, we are witnessing a new transformation within HPC. Quantum comput-
ing (QC) has emerged as a disruptive paradigm, expanding the concept of hetero-
geneous supercomputing architectures. Not only do traditional accelerators, such as 
GPUs and TPUs, remain integral to advanced computational ecosystems, but Quan-
tum Processing Units (QPUs) are also beginning to integrate into hybrid infrastruc-
tures. The combination of classical and quantum computing represents an expanding 
frontier where HPC, AI, and QC converge to tackle increasingly complex problems.
The recent study “Mapping the Landscape of Quantum Computing and High-
Performance Computing Research Over the Last Decade” [2] reinforces this per-
spective by analyzing the evolution of QC and HPC over the past decade. Through 
bibliometric analysis and scientific mapping, this work identifies how both fields

have gradually converged, with HPC playing a key role in quantum simulation 
and algorithm exploration. Furthermore, it highlights the increasing hybridization 
of classical and quantum infrastructures, consolidating the concept of heteroge-
neous supercomputing architectures. Its findings emphasize the impact of these 
technologies in fields such as optimization, machine learning, and cryptography, 
as well as the exponential growth of research in this domain.
The Journal of Supercomputing, recognizing the interrelation of these fields, 
has incorporated a new section: Quantum Computing, to aggregate research 
in this area and provide it with a dedicated context within the supercomputing 
domain. The year 2024 marks the beginning of this new endeavor.
This special issue reflects this evolution and brings together innovative 
research in these areas. Across the thirteen articles presented, advancements in 
computational architecture optimization, the efficient implementation of AI mod-
els in heterogeneous environments, and the challenges of applied quantum com-
puting are discussed.
In the field of quantum computing, contributions include new intermediate 
representations for quantum programming, efficient compilation of languages 
for distributed computing, and the integration of QPUs into HPC infrastructures. 
These studies are essential for the development of scalable architectures and the 
transition toward hybrid systems that combine the best approaches of classical 
and quantum computing.
Additionally, this volume includes research on optimizing performance in 
HPC environments through vectorization techniques, intelligent energy planning, 
and the containerization of scientific applications, improving the portability and 
reproducibility of computational experiments.
In the field of artificial intelligence and deep learning, techniques are explored 
for optimizing transformers in embedded systems, uncertainty reduction in dis-
tributed models, and leveraging accelerators such as GPUs to enhance perfor-
mance and energy efficiency.
Finally, studies addressing fundamental challenges in modern computing are 
included, such as channel estimation in sixth-generation (6 G) communication 
systems and the optimal selection of inter-GPU communication libraries in het-
erogeneous architectures. These works reflect the growing complexity of contem-
porary computational systems and the need for multidisciplinary approaches to 
their optimization.
We hope that the articles compiled in this issue provide the scientific com-
munity with valuable tools and insights to continue advancing research in these 
fields.
